newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-VW, IG Metall agree to wage pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-VW, IG Metall agree to wage pact.

text.p: Volkswagen AG and Germany's IG Metall said on Wednesday they have reached a comprehensive wage deal that gives the German carmaker the chance to pare its workforce through an early-retirement plan.

VW and IG Metall, the country's largest union, reached the deal late on Tuesday that calls for around 90,000 VW workers in west Germany to receive a 1.5 percent pay raise on August 1 and another 2.5 percent raise in August 1998.
The agreement also includes a pact for older workers at VW that IG Metall said was one of the first of its kind in Germany to reach a consensus over retirement issues.
VW said the early-retirement plan for workers aged 55 and older could affect about 10,000 people in the next five years at a cost to the carmaker of about 150,000 marks per worker.
The programme, which is retroactive to the start of 1997, calls for VW to help make up some of the lost wages for workers aged 55 and older who agree to voluntarily work part-time.
VW employees who agree to work part-time after age 55 would receive 85 percent of their wages through age 60 compared with the current level of 70 percent.
VW will also pay 100 percent of state pension benefit costs during the period of part-time work so that retirement benefits not be affected.

The deal will help VW cut it's payrolls without the carmaker having to resort to dramatic job cuts as technology gains reduce the amount of time needed to produce vehicles and the number of workers required on assembly lines.

In addition, VW is in the midst of a global expansion programme under which it is building new factories in lower-wage areas such as South America and Asia to grab a share of surging demand for new vehicles in emerging markets.
A VW spokesman said the early-retirement programme will also help allow VW to keep up to 1,000 trainees per year.
In addition to the wage increase and the retirement programme, the carmaker and IG Metall agreed that workers would also receive a 500 mark bonus in 1997.
Existing benefits for working on Saturdays will also remain but VW will have chance to integrate Saturday shifts into the normal working routine.
Three shifts could operate on Saturdays to help meet current strong demand for its cars and could help create new temporary jobs, VW negotiation leader Jochen Schumm said.
The wage contract runs through the end of July 1999, while a contract over job security issues runs through the end of 1999.
